planting.note: Plant small bulbs about 1 inch deep and 6-8 inches apart from late summer through fall; I'itoi goes summer-dormant in Gulf Coast heat and resprouts as temperatures cool, making fall the most reliable planting window.

directions: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them 6-8 inches apart to give clumps room to multiply. I'itoi is a heirloom perennial multiplier onion long cultivated by the Tohono O'odham of the Sonoran Desert borderlands, and it is unusual among onions for tolerating both intense summer heat and winter cold, which lets it persist as a perennial clump in Gulf Coast gardens rather than needing yearly replanting. A single planted bulb divides into eight or more bulbs within a season, and gardeners typically harvest by pulling scallion-like greens continuously while leaving part of the clump to keep multiplying underground. Dig and divide the clump when the foliage dies back in summer dormancy, replanting a portion immediately to keep the planting going indefinitely.
sources: Native Seeds/SEARCH — I'itoi Onion Growing Guide
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Pima County Master Gardener Program
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Aggie Horticulture Onion Growing Guide

planting.note: Direct sow from early spring into late spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; unlike most lettuce, Anuenue seed germinates readily even at soil temperatures above 80°F, which lets Gulf Coast gardeners sow it later into warming weather than typical lettuce varieties.

directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, thinning to 8-12 inches, and harvest as a full head once the center fills in. Anuenue was released by the University of Hawaii in 1987 specifically for tropical and subtropical climates, forming a small, crisp, iceberg-type head with bright green outer leaves and a well-packed pale heart, but with seed and heat tolerance far beyond typical crisphead lettuce. It is one of the few lettuce varieties whose seed will germinate reliably in hot soil rather than going dormant, and the plant resists developing the bitterness that ruins most lettuce as summer heat builds. For Gulf Coast gardeners this makes Anuenue a valuable bridge variety, extending fresh salad lettuce production later into late spring and earlier into late summer than standard cool-season types allow.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources (CTAHR) — Lettuce for the Home Garden
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

planting.note: Direct sow in spring, summer, or fall; Sparx holds its upright heart shape and resists bolting and bitterness in warm conditions better than standard romaine, making it a useful choice for extending the Gulf Coast lettuce season into late spring.

directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil, thinning to 8-12 inches, and harvest whole hearts once the upright heads have filled out. Sparx is a modern romaine bred for the fresh-market 'hearts' trade, producing dense, uniform, upright heads of crisp, sweet leaves on a plant noted for holding quality through hot spells that cause many other romaine types to turn bitter or bolt prematurely. Its dependable performance across spring, summer, and fall plantings makes it a practical choice for Gulf Coast gardeners looking to stretch romaine production beyond the short cool-season window most lettuce requires. Provide light afternoon shade during the hottest stretches to further slow bolting and preserve leaf quality.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

common_name: BHN 602 Tomato (Heat-Set Disease-Resistant Gulf South Hybrid)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and set out transplants once soil has warmed; BHN 602 was bred in Florida specifically to keep setting fruit through the high heat and humidity that stall many other slicing tomatoes.

directions: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, staking or caging to support the compact determinate vines. BHN 602 is a Florida-bred hybrid slicing tomato carrying a strong disease package — resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, and tomato spotted wilt virus — that holds up well against the soilborne and thrips-vectored diseases common in humid Gulf South gardens. The plants produce large, firm, deep-red, globe-shaped fruit averaging 10-12 ounces with good flavor for a hybrid of its size. It is widely recommended by Gulf South extension services as a reliable heat-set variety for both spring and fall planting windows, continuing to set fruit at temperatures that cause pollen sterility and blossom drop in less heat-adapted tomatoes.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Tomato Variety Recommendations
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Selector

common_name: BHN 968 Tomato (Heat-Tolerant Disease-Resistant Hybrid Cherry Tomato)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed; BHN 968 is rated among the most heat-tolerant cherry tomatoes in university trials, continuing to set fruit through the hottest stretch of a Gulf South summer.

directions: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the compact determinate plants to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. BHN 968 produces abundant clusters of small, shiny, deep-red cherry tomatoes prized for being notably sweeter and better textured than most determinate cherry types, backed by broad resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, tobacco mosaic virus, tomato spotted wilt virus, and root-knot nematodes. Its combination of compact habit, disease resistance, and standout heat tolerance makes it a dependable producer through the peak of Gulf Coast summer, when many indeterminate cherry varieties slow down or drop blossoms. Harvest continuously as fruit ripens to encourage ongoing production through the warm season.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Tomato Variety Recommendations
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

common_name: Magnolia Blackeye Cowpea (Disease-Resistant Mississippi Blackeye Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; Magnolia Blackeye was bred at Mississippi State University for resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode, both persistent problems in warm, sandy Gulf South garden soils.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, checking plants regularly since pods are not always held well above the foliage and can be easy to miss at harvest. Magnolia Blackeye is a Mississippi State University release bred from a cross involving Extra Early Blackeye, Bunch Purple Hull, and Dixielee, combining a compact, medium-sized bush habit with strong resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode along with tolerance to common cowpea viruses. Pods are light green-yellow at the green-shell stage, holding cream-to-light-green peas marked with the classic black eye, and the seed coat is notably smoother and less wrinkled than most other blackeye-type southern peas. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix nitrogen, and the plant's disease resistance package makes it a practical choice for Gulf South gardens where nematode or wilt pressure has limited other blackeye varieties.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension Service — Southern Pea Variety Recommendations
